how-an-os-is-organised.overview: An operating system is the layer that owns the hardware and decides who gets to use it. Almost every security boundary you rely on is a decision this layer makes on your behalf.
how_it_works: The kernel runs with full privilege and is the only component that talks directly to hardware.
Everything above it, including every application, runs as an unprivileged process with restricted access.
A user account and a process identity are separate, but both are checked before privileged operations are allowed.
The filesystem stores data and metadata together, so ownership and permissions travel with the file itself.
Memory is allocated in separated regions per process, and the enforcement of that separation is the core of process isolation.
history: Batch systems gave one user the whole machine, so the operating system was mainly a scheduler.
Timesharing and then personal computing introduced the need to separate users from each other.
The Unix permission model became the basis for a portable approach to file and process security that Windows also partly adopted.
Hardware support for virtualisation made it practical to run whole operating systems isolated from one another.
real_world: A service running as root has no meaningful boundary, so a flaw in it is effectively a flaw in the whole system.
A file copied to another user still carries its original owner and mode, which is why copied files can become more or less exposed.
A crash in one process should not affect another, and when it does the isolation model is not doing its job.
what_to_look_for: Check which user each critical service runs as, and whether that is the least privileged option that works.
Check the permissions on files holding credentials, configuration and keys.
Notice setuid and setgid bits, which change the effective user of a program and deserve explicit review.
Check whether sensitive data is separated from unprivileged users in memory as well as on disk.
defensive: Run each service under its own dedicated, unprivileged account.
Grant the minimum permissions needed and review anything with elevated file attributes.
Separate sensitive data with operating system controls rather than relying on application logic.
Patch the operating system itself, since kernel flaws undermine every isolation guarantee above it.

windows-security-model.overview: Windows security is built around access tokens, integrity levels and objects that list who may do what. Most Windows privilege escalation is a mismatch between those and how an application actually uses them.
how_it_works: Every logged-in session has an access token describing the user, their groups and their privileges.
Access checks compare that token against the access control list on each object, so the same user has different access to different objects.
Integrity levels add a second dimension, separating what an ordinary process may read from what a service may write.
User Account Control runs most of the desktop as a filtered standard-user token and only elevates specific operations.
Active Directory extends the same model to identities across a network, which is why a local account problem can become a domain one.
history: Windows NT replaced the older Windows with an explicit security model, including objects, tokens and descriptors.
User Account Control arrived because the standard user and administrator split was routinely undermined by applications requesting elevation constantly.
Active Directory and Group Policy turned Windows identity into the standard way large organisations manage access.
Later integrity levels, mandatory integrity control and virtualization-based security narrowed the paths from a compromised process to the system.
real_world: An application configured to run with full administrator rights loses every boundary the operating system would otherwise provide.
A service account with domain administrator rights turns one application flaw into a domain compromise.
A stored credential on a machine can be extracted and replayed, which is why the operating system tries to limit where it can be used.
what_to_look_for: Check whether any application is configured to run as administrator, and remove it if it can run without.
Check which accounts are in the local administrators group, since membership is persistent across restarts.
Notice stored credentials and machine account passwords, which are high-value targets.
Check that privileged actions require elevation rather than being silently performed.
defensive: Run day-to-day work as a standard user and elevate only for specific, visible operations.
Use separate, least-privileged service accounts rather than reusing an administrator account.
Restrict who can join local administrators and review that membership regularly.
Enable credential protection features your version supports, so stored secrets are harder to extract.
Treat any single point of failure account in the administrators group as a priority for review.

linux-permissions-users-groups.overview: Linux file permissions and ownership are simple enough to reason about in full. That simplicity is the point: a reviewer can usually tell whether an access decision is correct just by looking.
how_it_works: Every file has an owner, a group and a set of permission bits for the owner, the group and everyone else.
Directory permissions mean something different from file permissions: read lists names, write creates or deletes entries, and search permits traversal.
Processes run with a user and a group, and may temporarily gain additional groups.
Special permissions such as setuid and setgid change the effective identity used for access decisions.
Access is decided on the path, so a directory without search permission blocks access to everything beneath it.
history: The Unix permission model was designed to be understandable, with three classes and three bits rather than a growing access control list.
Access control lists and mandatory access control were later added for cases the simple model could not express.
Container platforms rely heavily on user namespaces and capabilities, which extend the model rather than replace it.
Modern distros ship with additional confinement features because the simple model has known gaps.
real_world: A world-readable private key file is one of the most common and most avoidable exposures on a Linux server.
A service running as root does not benefit from any file permission restriction, so a single flaw has full effect.
A directory with write permission for a group lets any member rename or delete files beneath it, regardless of the file's own permissions.
what_to_look_for: Look for world-readable files that should be restricted, especially keys and configuration with secrets.
Check which user each service runs as, and whether it has the privileges it actually needs.
Review setuid and setgid bits, since they change effective identity silently.
Check directory permissions, because they can grant or remove access regardless of the files inside.
defensive: Restrict sensitive files to their owning user, and verify with an unprivileged account rather than by eye.
Run services as dedicated unprivileged users, and use capabilities for specific privileges instead of running as root.
Review setuid and setgid entries, and remove any that are not clearly required.
Use directories to apply default permissions to new files, so correct access is inherited rather than remembered.
Audit with a listing of ownership and mode rather than trusting the intentions of whoever created the file.

command-line-for-security-work.overview: The command line is where security work becomes precise. It is also where mistakes have immediate effect, so the same power that makes it useful makes it worth treating carefully.
how_it_works: Commands read arguments and options, and the shell interprets quoting, expansion and redirection before anything runs.
Privilege is inherited, so a command run as root affects the system and not just a user session.
A pipeline passes output from one command to another, which is fast to write and hard to read later.
History and shell logging record what was typed, so a secret passed on the command line can persist on disk.
Scripting multiplies whatever habits you have, including the habits of skipping verification.
history: Unix treated small composable tools as the primary interface, which is why its tooling is scriptable by default.
Windows gained a capable command shell but most system administration still happened through a graphical console.
Container and orchestration tooling moved much of operations back to the command line out of necessity.
Remote execution tools now make it routine to run administrative commands across many machines, which raises the cost of a mistake.
real_world: A destructive command with a wildcard can remove far more than intended, and shell completion makes the wrong path easier to select.
A password typed as a command argument appears in shell history, in process listings and in any command log.
Piping output into a shell that interprets it turns a data source into a way to execute commands.
what_to_look_for: Prefer running a command that reports what it will do before one that changes anything.
Check whether a destructive command has a dry-run or confirmation option, and use it.
Avoid passing secrets on the command line, and use an input mechanism that does not record them.
Re-read any command you are about to run as an administrator, since the blast radius is the whole system.
defensive: Use the least privileged account that can complete the task, and escalate only for the specific step that needs it.
Pass secrets through standard input or a file with tight permissions, not as arguments.
Read scripts before running them, and treat a script from the internet as unreviewed code.
Keep a written record of administrative commands, because the shell history is not an audit log.
Use version control for configuration changes so a mistake is reversible.

processes-services-and-persistence.overview: A running program is a process, and a process that should survive a reboot is usually a service. Attackers establish persistence here, so understanding how things start is how you find what should not be running.
how_it_works: A process has a parent, a user, open files and network connections, and all of that is visible to an administrator.
A service is a process the operating system starts automatically and restarts when it exits.
Persistence is usually a scheduled task, a startup folder entry, a new service registration or a modified startup script.
The order in which the system starts these things defines a race, and attackers often aim to win it.
Every persistence mechanism leaves a record in a specific place, which is why enumerating those places is high value.
history: Manual startup scripts were the original persistence mechanism and are still widely used and widely abused.
The Windows registry became a convenient hiding place, and remains one of the most common.
Scheduled tasks added reliable recurring execution, and became a standard offensive technique.
Modern endpoint tooling watches these locations continuously, which raised the bar for staying hidden.
real_world: A service running from a user profile directory rather than a system path is unusual and worth investigating.
A scheduled task that runs a script from a temporary location is a common persistence mechanism after an initial compromise.
A process with no parent, or with a parent that has already exited, suggests it was started in an unusual way.
what_to_look_for: Enumerate services, scheduled tasks and startup entries on a regular schedule and compare against a known baseline.
Check what account each service runs as and what it executes.
Notice binaries running from temporary, download or user-writable directories.
Look for processes with no parent process, which can indicate injection or manual start.
defensive: Baseline services, scheduled tasks and startup entries, and alert on changes.
Restrict who can create or modify services and scheduled tasks, since both are privileged operations.
Keep administrative tooling and temporary directories out of the search path for services.
Prefer a service account with no interactive logon, so a compromised service cannot be used to log in.
Investigate unsigned or unexpectedly named binaries that start automatically.

logs-and-event-management.overview: The operating system records what happened. If nobody collects, keeps and reads those records, an incident investigation is limited to whatever a user reports.
how_it_works: Each platform has its own event log format and its own idea of what is worth recording by default.
Default logging usually records failures well and successes poorly, which is a problem when investigating misuse.
Authentication events are the most commonly needed, and are also the most commonly not recorded completely.
Logs are only useful if they survive the attack, so they belong somewhere an administrator cannot casually delete them.
Time matters: if clocks disagree, correlating records from different systems becomes guesswork.
history: Event logging on personal systems was minimal and locally controlled by the user.
Organisations adopted central logging mainly to satisfy audits rather than to detect attacks.
The realisation that an attacker with local administrator access can usually clear local logs drove adoption of centralised collection.
Detection engineering later shifted the goal from storing logs to using them to generate useful alerts.
real_world: A ransomware incident becomes far easier to scope when authentication logs survived and were sent off the host.
A single failed login three years after the fact is the only evidence of an intrusion that was never detected.
A system whose clock drifted produces an audit trail that appears internally consistent and is entirely wrong.
what_to_look_for: Check which event categories are recorded, and whether successful logins are included as well as failures.
Check where logs are stored and whether a local administrator can delete them.
Check clock synchronisation across systems whose records you intend to correlate.
Check the retention period, and whether it matches the time an investigation might realistically take.
defensive: Centralise log collection so an attacker with host access cannot erase the record.
Enable logging for administrative actions, privilege changes and successful authentications.
Synchronise time across systems, because unsynchronised logs cannot be correlated reliably.
Set retention to match or exceed the longest realistic investigation window.
Alert on the events that indicate a problem, because an unread log is an archive rather than a control.

patching-and-vulnerability-management.overview: Patching closes known weaknesses. What matters is not the volume of updates applied but whether the ones that matter reached the systems that are actually exposed.
how_it_works: A vulnerability has a severity rating and a known fix, and both depend on context you have to supply.
Prioritisation should weigh exposure and what the weakness allows, not just the published score.
A system that cannot be patched can often be mitigated by configuration, segmentation or monitoring instead.
Applications and their dependencies are usually a larger source of risk than the operating system itself.
A patch process that can be bypassed quietly is not a patch process, and this is where attackers actually work.
history: Patching was a periodic, largely manual activity tied to operating system releases.
Attackers standardised on exploiting the gap between disclosure and deployment, and that gap still drives most intrusion.
Software composition analysis brought third-party components into scope, which sharply increased the visible volume of findings.
Modern approaches attempt to make patches hard to bypass, treating the update channel itself as privileged infrastructure.
real_world: An internet-facing system missing a critical update is the most common finding in external assessments.
A build pipeline that lets a developer bypass the security step makes every policy a suggestion.
A component that is no longer maintained will never receive a fix, so something else has to compensate.
what_to_look_for: Know your inventory first, since you cannot patch a system you do not know exists.
Check which systems are internet-reachable and compare that against their patch level.
Check third-party and open-source dependencies, which are frequently older than the application code.
Check whether the update path itself requires an account with administrative rights, since that is where bypasses happen.
defensive: Prioritise by exposure and impact, and record the reasoning for anything deferred.
Patch internet-facing systems on a short timescale and internal systems on a longer one.
Remove software that is unmaintained rather than hoping it stays safe.
Restrict and monitor the update channel so it cannot be bypassed quietly.
Rebuild from known-good images periodically, since long-lived machines drift from their original state.

endpoint-protection-av-edr.overview: Endpoint protection has moved from scanning for known bad files to watching behaviour. The change is significant: detection now depends on what a process does, not only what it is called.
how_it_works: Antivirus compares files against known-bad signatures and reputation, which works well for known threats.
Behavioural detection watches a process tree and its actions, and can flag a novel program doing something suspicious.
Endpoint detection and response additionally records activity centrally, so an investigation is not limited to one machine.
Application control allows only approved programs to run, which removes whole categories of risk at the cost of flexibility.
Cloud-delivered lookup improves detection latency, which is why a machine that has been offline is a blind spot.
history: Signature-based antivirus dominated for two decades and worked well against the threat model it was built for.
Polymorphic and packed malware defeated signatures, and heuristics were added to compensate.
Fileless techniques, which run entirely in memory, broke file scanning almost entirely and drove behavioural approaches.
Managed detection and response added human analysts on top of telemetry, because tooling alone does not keep up.
real_world: A system with endpoint protection disabled is often disabled to make a specific application work, which removes the control permanently.
Allow-listing one folder for an installer can become a permanent gap in a policy that was meant to be temporary.
A detection that fires constantly and is always ignored teaches everyone to ignore it, which is worse than not having it.
what_to_look_for: Check whether endpoint protection is actually running and reporting, not merely installed.
Check for exclusions, since each one is a deliberate hole in the control.
Check whether telemetry is reaching the central system, since local-only logs are lost if the host is reimaged.
Check how many alerts are open and how long they have been open.
defensive: Keep endpoint protection enabled and reporting centrally, and treat disabling it as an exception with an expiry date.
Minimise exclusions, and document why each is needed.
Enable behavioural detection and application control where the environment supports it.
Tune alerts so the ones that matter are not buried, and measure how long a real alert takes to be actioned.
Keep definitions and platform current, since old signatures protect against old threats only.

hardening-a-fresh-install.overview: Hardening a new system means removing what you do not need, restricting what remains, and turning on the logging that tells you what happens later. The order matters, because each step reduces the next.
how_it_works: Start from a documented baseline rather than from defaults, so the result is reproducible and reviewable.
Remove unnecessary software, accounts and services, because every one of them is a future maintenance and attack obligation.
Restrict administrative access to named accounts, and remove shared or default ones.
Turn on the logging and monitoring that you will want during an incident, before you need it.
Apply configuration as code so the baseline can be rebuilt and compared, rather than drifting machine by machine.
history: Early hardening was a checklist applied once to individual machines, with no way to verify it stayed applied.
Configuration management made baselines repeatable, and compliance frameworks provided the specific settings to apply.
Cloud platforms shifted part of the control from the machine to the platform, changing what a baseline even means.
Current practice treats a hardened image as a build artifact that is rebuilt regularly rather than a machine that is patched indefinitely.
real_world: A default administrator account with a known password left enabled is still one of the most common serious findings.
A server that does not need to be on the internet should not be, and removing that requirement removes a whole class of exposure.
A hardened baseline applied once and never verified gives false confidence, because configuration drift is continuous.
what_to_look_for: Check which accounts can administer the system and whether each one is still needed.
Check which services are running and whether the software is still supported.
Check whether the documented baseline actually matches what is deployed.
Check that logging and time synchronisation are enabled before an incident, not during one.
defensive: Define a documented baseline and enforce it automatically rather than by hand.
Remove default accounts, sample applications and unused network listeners.
Require multi-factor authentication for every administrative path, including ones only reachable internally.
Enable logging for authentication, privilege changes and administrative actions from the start.
Rebuild machines from hardened images periodically, so drift is corrected by replacing rather than by patching.
